audit_method: Read-only git show v0.7.2:<path> against the exact tagged source; the newer working-tree source was not used.
scope: Public bmm_fp8 backend=cublas and shared autotuner; interpretation aid only, no batch-result or performance conclusion.

facts.fact: bmm_fp8 with backend=cublas obtains the cached workspace/module, enters fp8_gemm_sm100, constructs a new CublasFp8GemmRunner, calls choose_one, then executes the chosen runner. The module factory is cached; the runner instance is not.

Each runner starts with an empty _algo_cache. _get_algos caches by full A/B shapes and A/B/output dtypes. On a miss it allocates a CPU uint8 algorithm buffer, invokes native enumeration, and stores the resulting buffer/count. get_valid_tactics returns ordinal indexes range(count).

TunableRunner.__hash__ skips attributes ending in _cache. The per-instance algorithm cache therefore does not by itself change runner hash identity when populated. This is separate from the autotuner winner cache.

A nonnegative tactic reuses or fills _algo_cache, dispatching module.bmm_fp8_run_with_algo only when the ordinal is in range. Tactic -1, and out-of-range explicit ordinals, use module.bmm_fp8. A logged ordinal alone does not prove an explicit algorithm executed unless runtime eligibility is also checked.

Native enumeration constructs cuBLASLt descriptors/preferences, requests up to 100 heuristic algorithms, and copies their algorithm structures into the CPU buffer. The explicit execution helper constructs descriptors and dispatches cublasLtMatmul with the selected structure; it performs no additional heuristic query inside that helper.

The native default helper constructs descriptors/preferences and requests exactly one heuristic result before calling cublasLtMatmul. Thus -1 bypasses Python multi-result enumeration, but does not bypass all CPU heuristic work. Code alone does not establish that its selected algorithm is identical to ordinal 0 from a multi-result query.
The native bindings reuse thread-local cuBLASLt handles by device. Per-call descriptor/query work and per-runner algorithm-list caching must not be confused with handle creation on every invocation.

On a profile-cache miss, choose_one synthesizes inputs, enumerates valid tactics, and performs precompilation/preparation before entering the per-tactic _profile_single_kernel loop. For this runner, enumeration primes its retained algorithm cache. The generic preparation call uses tactic=-1 and do_preparation=True, so v1 can execute the default path without profiling it as a competing candidate.

Inside v2, choose_one prepends -1 for the first runner if it is absent. It checks the profile cache before candidate enumeration. This adds a measured candidate on misses; it does not force already-cached winners to be compared again.

The FP8 GEMM config specifies shape bucketing/constraints but no timing overrides. TuningConfig defaults use_cuda_graph=False and use_cold_l2_cache=False. With no measurement policy or other override, this operation uses the hot/eager profiling route. These source defaults should be cross-checked against the recorded effective config.

The tuner defaults to three warmup calls, ten profiling repeats, and a 5000-us stream delay for the non-graph route. Warmup is outside timing. The hot route records GPU events or device globaltimer timestamps around repeated retained-runner calls and divides GPU elapsed time by repeat count. A stream delay is inserted before the start marker unless events_no_delay is explicitly selected; its stated purpose is to hide host submission overhead. This is not public-API end-to-end wall timing, and delayed GPU timing is not an unconditional proof that no host submission gap remains.

When graph profiling is enabled, runner calls are captured before the timing markers, then the timed section replays the graph. Likewise, a public-call graph captured by a framework does not reconstruct the Python runner or re-enumerate algorithms on each replay. Host capture/setup cost must be distinguished from replay cost.

FP8 dynamic M uses the hybrid bucket mapper; output-M and workspace dimensions are wildcarded in the normalized cache key. Algorithm-list enumeration itself uses actual A/B shapes. Consequently normalized cache-key equality or an in-range ordinal is not evidence that a cuBLAS algorithm descriptor is identical across two actual M values.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Repeated runner construction, CPU algorithm-buffer allocation, multi-result querying and descriptor work may contribute to eager public-call differences between an explicit ordinal and -1. The retained, pre-enumerated profiling runner does not reproduce that complete eager path.
hypotheses.confirmation_needed: A separate CPU/API trace or controlled decomposition; GPU events spanning queued public calls may also contain host submission gaps.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A profiling winner, an eager public-call winner and a graph-replay winner may differ because their execution/timing boundaries differ. Source establishes the different boundaries, not their size or which candidate wins.
hypotheses.confirmation_needed: Independent eager and graph samples plus the actual selected runner/tactic, with matched inputs/cache provenance.

hypotheses.hypothesis: For an off-bucket runtime M, a persisted ordinal may select a different descriptor or have different timing than the profile probe. Runtime eligibility checks prevent known out-of-range fallback but do not establish descriptor identity.
hypotheses.confirmation_needed: Descriptor identity evidence or direct runtime candidate measurements; do not infer equivalence from ordinal equality alone.

limits: No GPU, remote, CI, analyzer, worker or repository-source changes were performed for this audit.
Source inspection does not establish actual heuristic count, kernel identity, latency, throughput, clock stability or universal v2 advantage.
Default -1 is a heuristic dispatch path, not a stable named cuBLAS algorithm.
Effective timer/config/source hashes in experiment results remain the authority for how a particular worker ran.
